claims.text: Controlled heat treatment and alloying can enhance the distribution of passive-element-rich precipitates in steel.
An enhanced distribution of passive-element-rich precipitates promotes formation of continuous and adherent passive oxide layers.
Continuous and adherent passive oxide layers lower steel corrosion rates by impeding corrosive species from reaching the substrate.
Standard steel alloys have compositions and microstructures that do not intentionally optimize passive-element distribution.
Heat-treatment and alloying adjustments can control the concentration and distribution of passive-element-rich precipitates.
Chromium-rich or other passive-element-rich precipitates serve as nucleation sites for passive oxide formation.
Under service conditions, passive-element-rich precipitates oxidize to form a continuous and adherent passive film.
The passive film acts as a physical barrier to corrosive species.
Barrier action by the passive film reduces corrosion attack.
Steels with enhanced, uniformly distributed passive-element-rich precipitates will form more robust oxide layers than standard steels under the same exposure conditions.
Steels with enhanced, uniformly distributed passive-element-rich precipitates will exhibit lower corrosion rates than standard steels under the same exposure conditions.
Standard compositions and untreated microstructures produce less protective, discontinuous oxide layers under the specified conditions.
The proposed mechanism requires steels to contain a minimum amount of passive element.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply under conventional chemical-processing and nuclear-power operating conditions.
Applicability may be limited under conditions substantially outside conventional chemical-processing and nuclear-power operating ranges.
The magnitude of corrosion-resistance improvement may vary with operating conditions and steel composition.
